entries.label: CPTS arsenal
entries.detail: Command-first pentest reference along the Cyber Kill Chain: search by port, service or tool

entries.label: CPTS: Reconnaissance
entries.detail: Map the target: hosts, open ports, services, versions, and the people and names around them. Passive OSINT first, then active scanning and enumeration.

entries.label: CPTS: Weaponisation
entries.detail: Turn a finding into something that will run on the target: a payload, a crafted document, a wordlist tuned to the environment.

entries.label: CPTS: Delivery
entries.detail: Get the payload or request to the target: a web request, an upload, a phishing email, a captured protocol.

entries.label: CPTS: Exploitation
entries.detail: Trigger the flaw and get first execution or access: a service exploit, a web vulnerability, a weak credential.

entries.label: CPTS: Installation
entries.detail: Make access durable and usable: a shell upgrade, a foothold, local privilege escalation, persistence.

entries.label: CPTS: Command & Control
entries.detail: Operate the foothold: a stable channel back to the operator, tasking, and tunnelling to reach deeper.

entries.label: CPTS: Actions on Objectives
entries.detail: Achieve the engagement goal: credential access, lateral movement, domain and data objectives, and the evidence for the report.

entries.label: AutoRecon: Automated recon orchestration
entries.detail: A multi-target recon orchestrator. It runs the port scan, then fires the right enumeration tool at each service it finds and files the output per host and port. Use it to get broad, structured coverage early so you can read while it works.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: feroxbuster: Recursive web content discovery
entries.detail: A fast, recursive directory and file brute-forcer. It walks into every directory it finds and keeps scanning, so a single run maps a whole site. Reach for it when a web port is open and gobuster or ffuf is leaving depth unexplored.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: ffuf: Web fuzzing
entries.detail: A fast web fuzzer that puts the FUZZ keyword anywhere in a request: paths, parameters, headers, POST bodies and Host for vhosts. The flexible companion to Gobuster when you need recursion, filtering or to fuzz something other than a path.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Gobuster: Web content discovery
entries.detail: Brute-forces hidden web content: directories and files, DNS subdomains, and virtual hosts. Run it against any HTTP or HTTPS service once a port scan finds one.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Kerbrute: Kerberos user enumeration and spraying
entries.detail: Validates Active Directory usernames fast and quietly against the KDC (a bad username draws no logon failure), then sprays one password across the accounts that exist. The first move when you have a domain and a user list but no credentials yet.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: NetExec: Network and AD enumeration
entries.detail: The successor to CrackMapExec. Sweeps a subnet for SMB, WinRM, LDAP, MSSQL and more, checks credentials across hosts, lists shares and users, and flags where a credential is a local admin. The workhorse of internal and Active Directory enumeration.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Nmap: Network scanning
entries.detail: The port scanner. Finds live hosts, open ports, service versions and, through NSE scripts, a first pass of service enumeration. Usually the first command run against an in-scope network.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: RustScan: Fast port scanning
entries.detail: A very fast port sweep that finds the open ports in seconds, then hands them straight to Nmap for version and script scanning. Use it as the front end to Nmap when a full-range scan would otherwise be slow.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Service enumeration: Port by port enumeration cheat sheet
entries.detail: After the port scan, the first move on each open service. What to run against FTP, SSH, SMTP, DNS, SMB, SNMP, LDAP, MSSQL, NFS and the rest to pull users, shares, versions and config.
entries.words: FTP (21), SSH (22), SMTP (25) DNS (53) SMB (139/445) and RPC SNMP (161/udp), LDAP (389) NFS (2049), MSSQL (1433), MySQL (3306), RDP (3389), WinRM (5985) Notes

entries.label: msfvenom: Payload generation
entries.detail: The Metasploit payload generator. Produces reverse and bind shells in the format the target can run: exe, elf, war, aspx, raw shellcode: ready to pair with a listener. The standard way to make a payload for an authorised test.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: File transfer (web, SMB, FTP): Getting files on and off a host
entries.detail: The everyday ways to move a tool onto a target or pull loot back, over HTTP, SMB or FTP. Host a server on your box, then fetch or push from the target with what it already has.
entries.words: Pick a channel Host a server on your attacking box Windows: download Windows: upload Linux: download and upload Base64 copy and paste (no network) Notes

entries.label: File transfer with code: Download and upload with a language runtime
entries.detail: When the usual tools are missing but a language runtime is present. Python, PHP, Ruby, Perl, JavaScript and VBScript all run one-line downloaders, and Python also uploads.
entries.words: When to reach for it Download Windows with JavaScript or VBScript Upload with Python Notes

entries.label: Living off the land (LOLBAS / GTFOBins): Transfers with trusted built-in binaries
entries.detail: Using signed, already-installed binaries to pull or push files, so nothing new lands on disk and application whitelisting is less likely to block you. The LOLBAS (Windows) and GTFOBins (Linux) projects catalogue them.
entries.words: The idea Windows download Windows upload Linux (GTFOBins), openssl as an nc-style transfer Notes

entries.label: Protected and evasive transfers: Encrypting files and blending in
entries.detail: Encrypt sensitive data before it moves, and change the user agent so a transfer does not stand out. For exfil during an authorised test and for handling client data responsibly.
entries.words: Encrypt before it moves Blend the transfer in Notes

entries.label: Responder: LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning
entries.detail: Answers LLMNR, NBT-NS and mDNS name-resolution requests on the local segment, so a host looking for a mistyped or missing name connects to you instead and hands over an NTLMv2 hash. A top source of first credentials on an internal test.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Transfer when the web is blocked: Netcat, /dev/tcp, RDP and WinRM
entries.detail: Moving files without an HTTP or SMB server: a raw Netcat or /dev/tcp pipe, an RDP drive mount, or a PowerShell Remoting session. For when outbound web and SMB are filtered.
terms: transfer when the web is blocked
entries.words: Netcat / Ncat Bash /dev/tcp (no nc on the target) PowerShell Remoting (WinRM) RDP drive mount Notes

entries.label: Hydra: Credential attacks
entries.detail: Online password guessing against a live service: SSH, FTP, RDP, web login forms and many more. Use it for a targeted spray with a short, sensible list, not a blind dictionary run.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Metasploit Framework: Exploitation framework
entries.detail: The exploitation framework: a searchable library of exploits and payloads, the multi/handler that catches shells, Meterpreter for post-exploitation, and routing for pivoting. The hub that ties weaponisation, exploitation and C2 together.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Payloads: staged vs stageless Meterpreter: core post-exploitation Privilege escalation Credentials Pivoting Persistence (authorised engagements only) Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Reverse shells: Getting a shell back
entries.detail: Turning code execution into an interactive shell on your machine. Start a listener, fire a one-liner on the target, and catch the connection. The payloads that work when you already have a way to run a command.
entries.words: When to reach for it Start a listener Linux target one-liners Windows target one-liners Notes

entries.label: SearchSploit: Exploit lookup (Exploit-DB)
entries.detail: The command-line search for the offline Exploit-DB archive. Match a service and version from recon to a known public exploit, read it, and copy it out to work on. The bridge from "what version is this" to "is there an exploit".
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: sqlmap: SQL injection
entries.detail: Automates finding and exploiting SQL injection. Confirms the flaw, fingerprints the database, dumps data, and: where the configuration allows: reads files or gets command execution. Point it at a request you suspect is injectable.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Web attacks: LFI, upload, command injection, SSTI
entries.detail: The web flaws that turn a page into code execution or file read, beyond SQL injection. Local and remote file inclusion, upload bypasses, command injection and template injection, with the payloads to confirm each.
entries.words: Local / remote file inclusion (LFI/RFI) File upload bypass Command injection Server-side template injection (SSTI) Notes

entries.label: Linux privilege escalation: Local root on Linux
entries.detail: The checks that turn a user shell into root: sudo rights, SUID binaries, cron jobs, capabilities, writable files and PATH. Run the enumeration, then exploit the one good finding.
entries.words: Enumerate Common wins Notes

entries.label: PEASS-ng (linPEAS / winPEAS): Privilege escalation enumeration
entries.detail: The privilege-escalation scouts. linPEAS and winPEAS enumerate a host for local privesc routes: weak permissions, stored credentials, misconfigured services, sudo and SUID, scheduled tasks: and colour-code the most promising findings. Run one the moment you land a shell.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Shell upgrade (TTY): Stabilising a caught shell
entries.detail: Turning the dumb shell you just caught into a usable one: job control, tab completion, arrow keys, and a window size that does not break full-screen tools. The first thing to do after catching a Linux reverse shell.
entries.words: When to reach for it Linux: full TTY upgrade Linux: quick improvements (when a full TTY will not cooperate) Windows Notes

entries.label: Windows privilege escalation: Local admin / SYSTEM on Windows
entries.detail: Routes from a user shell to SYSTEM on Windows: token privileges, weak services, unquoted paths, AlwaysInstallElevated, stored credentials and autoruns. Enumerate, then take the one that fits.
entries.words: Enumerate Common wins Stored credentials Notes

entries.label: Chisel: Tunnelling and pivoting
entries.detail: A fast TCP/UDP tunnel over HTTP, in a single Go binary for every platform. Builds a SOCKS proxy or port-forward through a compromised host so your tools on the outside can reach an internal network you otherwise cannot touch.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: ligolo-ng: Tunnelling and pivoting
entries.detail: A VPN-style pivot. Instead of a SOCKS proxy and proxychains, it stands up a tun interface so your tools reach the internal network directly, at native speed and with no wrapper. The current go-to for pivoting once you have a foothold.
entries.words: When to reach for it The two pieces Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Pivoting and tunnelling: Reaching an internal network through a foothold
entries.detail: Using a compromised host to reach the network behind it. SSH port forwards, a SOCKS proxy through proxychains, or a userland VPN with Ligolo-ng, so your tools on the outside hit internal targets.
entries.words: SSH forwards proxychains Ligolo-ng (userland VPN, no proxychains) Notes

entries.label: Active Directory enumeration: Mapping the domain
entries.detail: Once you have any domain credential, map users, groups, computers, GPOs, trusts and the password policy. The data that drives every AD attack path.
entries.words: From Linux, with a credential From Windows, with PowerView What to look for Notes

entries.label: BloodHound: Active Directory attack paths
entries.detail: Maps Active Directory as a graph and finds the shortest path from where you are to Domain Admin. A collector (SharpHound or the Python collector) gathers users, groups, sessions, ACLs and trusts; BloodHound shows who can reach what, and how.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Evil-WinRM: Remote access (WinRM)
entries.detail: A clean interactive shell over WinRM (Windows Remote Management). Give it a password or an NTLM hash and, if the account is in Remote Management Users, you get a PowerShell session with handy upload, download and in-memory script loading built in.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Hashcat / John the Ripper: Offline hash cracking
entries.detail: Where captured hashes turn into passwords. Hashcat is the GPU workhorse; John covers odd formats, CPU cracking and the *2john extractors. The end of the credential-capture chain: Responder loot, Kerberoast tickets, shadow and KeePass files all land here.
entries.words: When to reach for it Identify the hash first Hashcat: key flags Hashcat: commands John: key flags and the *2john tools Workflow Notes

entries.label: Impacket: Windows and AD protocol tooling
entries.detail: A toolbox of Python scripts that speak Windows protocols directly. secretsdump pulls hashes, the exec scripts (psexec, wmiexec) give remote shells, and GetUserSPNs/GetNPUsers pull Kerberos tickets to crack. The backbone of Active Directory attacks from Linux.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes

entries.label: Kerberos attacks: Roasting, delegation and ticket abuse
entries.detail: Turning Kerberos into credentials and access: roast service and pre-auth-less accounts for offline cracking, then reuse tickets to move and persist. The core of the AD domain phase.
entries.words: Kerberoasting (service accounts) AS-REP roasting (no pre-auth) Pass / overpass the hash, and tickets Windows, with Rubeus Notes

entries.label: mimikatz: Windows credential dumping
entries.detail: The credential toolkit on Windows. Pull plaintext, hashes and Kerberos tickets from LSASS, dump the local SAM, DCSync a hash straight from a domain controller, and pass or forge tickets. Reach for it once you have admin on a Windows host.
entries.words: When to reach for it Key flags Commands Workflow Notes
